title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to test whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was deterministically reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style deterministic validator. All 200 shared initial candidates were scored valid by the validator in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; paired‑bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. We present the preregistered design and frozen execution accounting, an artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null result under shared_initial_candidate semantics, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that avoid ceiling effects and permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into concrete network device configurations and maintenance workflows. Operational deployment of such pipelines requires evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to live networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, accept/reject gates, and bounded repair loops—rather than on the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are recommended in both NetOps and adjacent domains, yet reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates remains limited [3],[4].

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) a confirmatory execution using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an interpretation of ceiling effects grounded in execution diagnostics; and (5) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that allow nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research covers intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, RCA, and emerging agentic automation proposals. Several recent surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, retrieval anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[2],[5]. In adjacent technical domains, generate–validate–repair pipelines have improved safety or repairability for program repair and DevOps tasks under specific datasets and validators [6],[7].

Methodological gaps. Two methodological limitations motivate a paired design that preserves initial sampling. First, pipeline comparisons that allow different first‑pass model draws per arm confound validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many existing benchmarks prioritize QA/relevance metrics or log/RCA tasks but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. The shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates the validator/gate effect on identical initial outputs, directly addressing the first gap and making explicit the estimand's conditional scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered under the identifier autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The preregistration fixed the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate, model/adaptor = gpt‑5‑mini via the hosted adapter, deterministic validator = a Batfish‑style deterministic_netops_validator (validator version 5.0), accept/reject gate and repair policy (maximum automated repair attempts per task = 1), deterministic task selection rule, sample size (200 paired intents), and the confirmatory analysis procedure (paired binary analysis with an exact two‑sided test and paired‑bootstrap percentile CI). These decisions were frozen prior to observing any model outputs.

Generation semantics and arms. The executed generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. Under these semantics the paired contrast evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or model sampling variance.

Models, validator, and task bank. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (hosted adapter). Deterministic validator: a Batfish‑style validator implementing sequencing and precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency rules. The synthetic task generator produced intent→configuration items with embedded constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies and explicit required_sequence lists). Task difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard", "extreme") were recorded during generation and the bank used deterministic seeds so selection is fixed and outcome‑independent.

Interventions, gating, and outcome. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without validator gating. Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to the deterministic validator; the gate followed a preregistered accept/reject rule and, upon violations, permitted up to one automated repair attempt. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization, scored using the validator's full_intent_constraint_validation rule and reported as VALID_CONFIGURATION or specific violation codes.

Confirmatory analysis. The preregistered confirmatory analysis compared unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs using a 2×2 paired contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00). The analysis reported discordant pair counts n10 (guarded_only) and n01 (baseline_only), an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729; resamples=10,000). The missingness policy was complete_pairs_primary; the run produced no retriable infrastructure failures.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The confirmatory run executed as preregistered and completed without episode failures. Planned_episode_count = 400 (two conditions per pair); completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0. Because of shared_initial_candidate semantics, one model call was made per pair: model_calls_used = 200. Provider auditing recorded 200 completed hosted model call events and no cache reuse across conditions.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency counts were n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. In other words, every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by the deterministic validator in both baseline and guarded arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The preregistered exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). The zero‑width CI and p = 1.0 are arithmetic consequences of complete concordance (no discordant pairs) under the registered estimand.

Repair activity and validator diagnostics. No automated repairs were applied for any guarded episode (repair_applied = false for all 200 guarded episodes). Representative episodes show that parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count matched task constraints, and validator violation_count = 0. For example, a representative task required four commands, the shared initial candidate contained four parsed commands, and validation_before/validation_after both reported valid = true with zero violations.

Provider audit, timing, and missingness. Provider audit counters show hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; cache_hit_count = 0. Median additional per‑pair wall time for the guarded arm was dominated by deterministic validator evaluation, and no repair cycles contributed to latency. Missingness_summary reports complete_pairs = 200 with zero failed or unscorable episodes.

Execution accounting consistency. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed episode accounting consistency and marginal contingency consistency between per‑condition summaries and the paired table. The run produced no infrastructure retries or condition contamination flags.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, given the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates satisfied the validator constraints and therefore the guarded machinery performed no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. With no discordant pairs every bootstrap resample of the paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0); this produces zero empirical variance and therefore a CI [0.0,0.0]. This is a legitimate inferential outcome rather than an analysis error.

Ceiling‑effect contributors. The execution diagnostics indicate three concrete, nonexclusive contributors to the ceiling effect: (1) task‑bank alignment—the synthetic generator produced intents whose required sequences closely matched the expected prompt schema, increasing the probability of syntactically correct model outputs; (2) validator tightness—the validator encoded the sequencing and precondition checks that aligned with the task generator's reference answers, so syntactically correct mappings passed validation readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics—reusing the same initial candidate for both arms precluded any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance that might have produced repairs or discordant outcomes. Each contributor is supported by per‑episode difficulty labels, required_sequence fields, and validator diagnostics recorded during the run.

Design recommendations to avoid ceiling effects. To permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value we recommend preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or introduce sampling variance: (a) augment the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates; (b) execute an alternative confirmatory design using independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple independent samples per condition to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model sampling variance, acknowledging the increased model_call accounting (up to two model calls per pair); (c) evaluate multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to reveal model variance effects; (d) expand the automated repair budget or enable iterative repair loops to assess repair effectiveness when initial violations are nontrivial; and (e) include human‑in‑the‑loop arms to measure operator responses to validator flags and real‑world triage decisions.

Operational implications and caveats. The observed null effect does not imply deterministic validators lack value in more realistic or adversarial regimes. Rather, it demonstrates that design choices (task bank, generation semantics, validator rules) determine whether a paired shared‑candidate contrast can detect verifier value. Our run shows that, for the chosen setup, initial generations were already validated by the deterministic ruleset. Field deployments should evaluate adversarial item injection, per‑condition independent sampling, and HITL arms before asserting operational benefits.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the identical initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator; the guarded pipeline applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank and task‑generation seeds, the deterministic validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent per‑condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple samples) [1]–[3],[6]. We archive full execution and analysis artifacts and recommend preregistered follow‑ups that intentionally produce nonzero baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside the validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0.0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect approximately 10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits such as reduced human triage time or deployment safety were not measured in this study.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was not used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: task difficulty metadata recorded during generation indicates the bank was dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme'; exact per‑label counts are available in the archived task manifest.
